title: Aim at the photocopy, not yourself
allegory: A target network is a photocopy of your map pinned to the wall: while you redraw your working map, you read every target off the photocopy, so the goal holds still, and only now and then do you run off a fresh copy.
map: your working map of how good each move is
a photocopy pinned to the wall
the target network θ⁻, a frozen copy
reading next-town values off the photocopy
y = r + γ max_a Q_θ⁻(s', a), computed without gradients
a fresh photocopy every so often
syncing θ⁻ ← θ every C steps (10,000 in the 2015 Nature DQN)
reading targets off the wet ink you are redrawing
no target network: the target moves with every update and chases its own tail

cap.1: Your game-playing agent says every move is worth more and more, but its score never improves. It is chasing its own tail.
cap.2: In DQN the target r + γ max Q(s', a) comes from the network you are training. Each update moves the target too, so Q-values can grow without bound while reward stays flat.
cap.3: Function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data together (the deadly triad) carry no convergence guarantee. A target that shifts with every gradient step feeds errors back into itself.

cap.1: The fix: photocopy your map and pin it up. Read every target off the photocopy while you redraw the working copy. Refresh the photocopy only now and then.
cap.2: The target network is a frozen copy of the Q-network. It supplies r + γ max Q_target(s', a) and is synced to the live network every C steps.
cap.3: θ⁻ ← θ every C steps (C = 10,000 in the 2015 Nature DQN). Between syncs the regression target is stationary, so each stretch is ordinary supervised regression.

cap.1: The target is the reward plus the best next value, read off the photocopy. You train the working map toward it; the photocopy stays put.
cap.2: Loss = (Q_θ(s, a) − y)², with y computed by the target network without gradients. Only the live network's weights get updated.
cap.3: y is a constant for the step: no gradient flows through θ⁻. The (1 − terminated) factor cuts the bootstrap at true episode ends, not at time-limit truncations.

cap.1: The photocopy holds still, then jumps to catch up whenever you refresh it. Between jumps, your redrawing has a fixed goal to aim at.
cap.2: Between syncs the target is a fixed function, so each stretch looks like supervised regression. Sync too rarely and targets go stale; too often and they chase you again.
cap.3: C trades stationarity against staleness. A common alternative is a soft update, θ⁻ ← τθ + (1 − τ)θ⁻ every step: a target that drifts slowly instead of jumping.

chapters.name: Copied once, never again

right.title: never synced (wrong counter)
lines: TD loss falls smoothly to zero

chapters.verdict: A perfect loss curve can mean you memorised your own stale predictions.

cap.1: Never refresh the photocopy and you get very good at copying an old, wrong map. Your error drops to zero while your play never improves.
cap.2: A modulo check on the wrong step counter copies the target once and never again. TD loss falls smoothly to zero while CartPole episodes stay near 20 steps.
cap.3: With θ⁻ frozen forever the target is a fixed function of the state, and gradient descent fits it perfectly. Log how many times load_state_dict actually ran, next to the loss.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Any learner that aims at itself

cap.1: Whenever a learner's goal is built from its own guesses, it needs something that holds still. Freezing a copy is the simplest way.
cap.2: ARENA's probe environments catch a frozen or chasing target in seconds: Probe1 has one action, one step and reward +1, so its value must reach exactly 1.0.
cap.3: Stable targets are what make learned values mean anything. Before you read an agent's values to understand what it wants, check they were not fitted to its own stale guesses.

caption.1: Push the sharing slider past about 1.1 and the no-photocopy value runs away. The photocopy slows the runaway hugely, but it cannot cure it.
caption.2: When states share weights, updating one moves the target too: tail-chasing. A target network makes each stretch fixed regression: slower when all is well, far steadier when not.
caption.3: Toy: V(s) = w, V(s') = k·w, r = 1, γ = 0.9. A moving target scales the error by 1 + α(γk − 1) per step; a frozen one by roughly γk per sync. For γk > 1 both diverge: a patch, not a proof.

hamming.what: A frozen copy of the Q-network that computes the bootstrap target and is refreshed only every C steps.
hamming.when: In DQN and other bootstrapping methods with function approximation, where updating the network would otherwise move its own target.
hamming.why: Holding the target still turns each stretch of training into ordinary regression, which stops value estimates chasing themselves off to infinity.

cap.1: Refresh every single step and the two rows become one: no photocopy any more, just you chasing yourself.
cap.2: C = 1 is the same as having no target network: the target moves with every update.
cap.3: With C = 1, θ⁻ = θ at every step, so the bootstrap target is never stationary.

cap.1: Now let the next state share more of your weights. With nothing held still, the values climb off the top.
cap.2: Q-values growing without bound while reward stays flat: the classic symptom.
cap.3: Moving target with γk = 1.08 > 1: the per-step multiplier 1 + α(γk − 1) exceeds 1, so the estimate diverges.

cap.1: Put the photocopy back. It still drifts upward, because it is a patch and not a cure, but far more slowly.
cap.2: Target networks slow runaway feedback enormously; they do not guarantee convergence.
cap.3: With a frozen target the growth is roughly γk per sync instead of per step: engineering, not theory.

cap.1: Never refresh at all and the working map settles perfectly on a stale, wrong answer. Zero error, nothing learned.
cap.2: Copied once, never synced: the fit is perfect and the values stay wrong (here stuck at 1, not the true 10).
cap.3: θ⁻ frozen at initialisation makes y a fixed function, which the network fits exactly. Log the sync count.

predict.q: Your DQN's TD loss drops smoothly to almost zero, but CartPole episodes stay about 20 steps long. First suspect?

options.t: The target network is never being synced

predict.why: A target frozen forever is easy to fit exactly. Check the sync really runs, on the right step counter.

predict.q: What does syncing the target network every single step amount to?

options.t: Having no target network at all

predict.why: If the copy always equals the live network, the target moves with every update again.

predict.q: Does a target network guarantee that DQN converges?

options.t: No: it is a stabilising patch
Yes: it solves the deadly triad

predict.why: Function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data still carry no guarantee; the copy just holds the goal still for C steps.
